quote: Kann man durch eine endliche Anzahl solcher Operationen [-aus-] der identische Transformation $x = x$, $y = y$, sämmtliche [-...-] ableiten.
english: Can one derive all of them from the identical transformation x = x, y = y by a finite number of such operations?
topic: The page first builds a slowly growing function f(n) from iterated logarithms. It then asks whether all one-to-one analytic transformations of the plane can be generated from simple operations such as (u, v) → (u, v f(u)), noting that this gives transcendental one-to-one transformations.

triage.modern_statement: Read in modern terms, Hilbert is asking whether the group Aut(C^2) of biholomorphic self-maps of C^2 is generated by elementary triangular maps. These are 'overshears' such as (u,v) -> (u, v·e^{g(u)}) and 'shears' such as (u,v) -> (u, v + f(u)), with f and g entire, together with affine maps or coordinate swaps. In other words: can every holomorphic automorphism of the plane be written as a finite composition of such maps, starting from the identity? This is the question Rosay and Rudin later asked. The fully algebraic version, where all maps are polynomial, is the question of whether plane polynomial automorphisms are 'tame'.
triage.answered_by: Erik Andersén and László Lempert answered it in the negative (published 1992, with related work around 1989/90). The group generated by shears and overshears in C^n (n>=2) is dense in Aut(C^n), but it is a meagre proper subgroup, so some holomorphic automorphisms are not finite compositions of these maps, even for n=2. For polynomial automorphisms of the plane the answer is yes: Jung (1942) and van der Kulk (1953) proved every one is a finite composition of affine and triangular maps.

evidence.claim: Andersén and Lempert answered the Rosay–Rudin question with no: the group generated by shears and overshears in C^n is meagre in the holomorphic automorphism group, even for n=2.
Andersén and Lempert's 1992 discovery was that the group generated by shears is dense in Aut(C^n) for n>1. This is described as having had a fundamental impact.

Prompted by a question Walter Rudin promoted, Andersén and Lempert showed that the group generated by shears and overshears is dense in the holomorphic automorphism group of C^n (n>=2). This grew into the 'density property' theory.
Jung–van der Kulk theorem: every polynomial automorphism of C^2 is a finite composition of affine and triangular automorphisms, i.e. it is tame.

triage.why: The page describes one-to-one analytic, possibly transcendental, maps of the plane built from operations like (u,v)->(u, v f(u)) and asks whether finitely many such operations generate all of them. That matches the generation question for Aut(C^2) by shears and overshears. Andersén–Lempert settled that question negatively: the generated group is dense but a meagre proper subgroup, so 'all' fails if only finite compositions are allowed. The question is not among Hilbert's 23 published problems. The sources I found trace it to Rosay–Rudin and Walter Rudin, not to Hilbert, and I found nothing linking it to his notebook. Confidence is medium for two reasons. Hilbert's exact set of permitted operations, and whether he meant entire automorphisms of C^2, have to be inferred from a short note. Also, if he meant only polynomial or algebraic maps, the answer would be the positive Jung–van der Kulk theorem. The area is still active: Andersén–Lempert theory, the density property, and the tame/wild automorphism problems in dimension 3 and higher are current research topics.
